title: Private Deployments: VPC & On-Prem Operational + Reference Guide
author: Aisha Khan
summary: Comprehensive operational guide for private deployments (VPC and on-prem). Covers reference architectures, packaging, deployment checklist, day-2 operations, and upgrade/rollback procedures. Intended for SREs, Solutions Engineers, and customer technical leads.
body:
Overview:

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's recommended practices, runbooks, and reference configurations for Private deployments (VPC and on-prem). It is written for operators and customer engineering teams performing initial deployments and day-2 operations. Contents are normative where called out.

Sections:
1) Reference architectures
2) Packaging & installation patterns (on-prem)
3) VPC deployment checklist and network/security requirements
4) Day-2 operations and runbooks (backup, scaling, monitoring)
5) Upgrade and rollback procedures (minor/major)
6) Customer requirements library (preflight)
7) Ownership and escalation
8) Appendices: example manifests, sample SLOs, and common troubleshooting commands

1) Reference architectures

Purpose: provide validated topologies for common customer footprints (small, medium, large). Each reference notes control plane placement, data plane options, and high-availability patterns.

- Small (proof-of-concept): single-region VPC or single-rack on-prem; 2 control-plane nodes (HA via leader election), 1-2 worker GPU nodes. No cross-region failover. Intended for dev/test or pilot customers with non-critical SLAs.
- Medium (production): multi-AZ VPC or multi-rack on-prem; 3 control-plane nodes, dedicated GPU worker pool with autoscaling group, separate persistent storage tier for model artifacts and KV caches. Cross-AZ load balancing with regional failover.
- Large (enterprise/DR): multi-region VPC or multi-datacenter on-prem; active-passive control planes in regions with global DNS failover, geo-replicated object store for artifacts, capacity pools for hot/warm/cold models, and a policy-driven router for latency/cost-based routing.

Reference component map (narrative):
- Control plane: Kubernetes cluster (managed or self-hosted) running Redwood control-plane services (auth, config, operator). Requires TLS PKI and KMS integration for secrets.
- Data plane (serving runtime): GPU-attached node pool running the Redwood runtime as a DaemonSet or deployment depending on hardware topology. Use node labels to isolate dedicated capacity.
- Artifact store: S3-compatible object store (MinIO on-prem or cloud S3) for model blobs and quantization artifacts.
- Redis/KV cache: optional prefix/KV cache for low-latency reuse; HA cluster with persistence (e.g., Redis cluster with AOF).
- Observability: Prometheus + Thanos (metrics), Loki for logs, and Jaeger/OpenTelemetry traces.

2) Packaging & installation patterns (on-prem)

Supported packaging options:
- Helm chart (Kubernetes): primary supported path for on-prem and VPC Kubernetes clusters.
- OVA/container-runtime bundle: for air-gapped deployments where customers run a small hypervisor-based appliance.
- Systemd + containerd: minimal-host installs for bare-metal where customers prefer orchestration via systemd units.

Pre-install checks (example):
- Confirm GPU drivers and CUDA/cuDNN versions: NVIDIA driver 535.x, CUDA 12.1 compatible.
- Verify kernel modules: nvidia-smi reports expected devices.
- Verify storage: POSIX-compatible NFS for model cache is acceptable; object store recommended for artifact durability.

Install (Helm) - Example steps:
1. Add Redwood Helm repo: helm repo add redwood https://helm.redwood.ai/charts
2. Create namespace and secrets: kubectl create ns redwood-private; kubectl create secret generic redwood-kms --from-literal=key=<kms-endpoint>
3. Customize values.yaml (see Appendix A example) - set nodeSelector, tolerations, storage endpoints, and KMS config.
4. Install: helm install redwood-controlplane redwood/controlplane -n redwood -f values.yaml
5. Verify: kubectl get pods -n redwood --watch and ensure control-plane and runtime pods reach Ready state.

Packaging notes for air-gapped installs:
- Provide pre-pulled OCI bundle and a signed checksums manifest.
- Include offline Helm index and an offline artifact store (tarball of images + models).

3) VPC deployment checklist and network/security requirements

Network requirements (minimum):
- Subnets: dedicated subnets for control-plane, serving nodes, and management (jump hosts).
- Security groups / firewall rules: allow intra-cluster control-plane ports (TCP 6443, 2379-2380 for etcd if used), serving ports (customizable; default 8080/8443), healthcheck ports, and monitoring (Prometheus scrape).
- NAT / egress: serving nodes may require egress to model artifact store endpoints and metrics exporters.
- Route table and cross-AZ connectivity: low-latency (≤2ms) preferred between control-plane and serving nodes for KV cache coherence.

Security & compliance:
- TLS everywhere: mTLS enforced between services; control-plane issues short-lived certs.
- KMS integration: customer-managed key wrapping (KMS/HSM) for model secrets and audit logs.
- RBAC: map Redwood operators to a dedicated service account with least privilege; provide an example IAM policy in Appendix B.
- Audit logging: centralize API audit logs to S3-compatible archive with retention policy defined by customer compliance (default 90d).

Network checklist (operator):
1. Confirm VPC CIDR and expected pod/service CIDRs will not overlap on customer VPNs.
2. Provision subnets, route tables, and security groups per topology.
3. Validate route tables and NAT/gateway configuration for artifact store access.
4. Configure DNS and TLS certs for control-plane and API endpoints.

4) Day-2 operations and runbooks

Goals: keep platform healthy, scale capacity predictably, back up critical state, and provide reliable support handoff to customers.

Operational runbooks (short forms):
- Service health check (when control-plane degraded):
  1) Confirm API availability: curl -k https://redwood-api.local/healthz (expected: 200 and JSON containing component statuses).
  2) Check control-plane pods: kubectl -n redwood get pods -o wide. Identify CrashLoopBackOff and capture logs: kubectl logs <pod> -n redwood --previous.
  3) Check etcd/DB connectivity: kubectl exec -n redwood <db-pod> -- pg_isready or etcdctl endpoint health.
- Scaling GPU worker pool (manual):
  1) Evaluate current token throughput and pending request queue (observability dashboard).
  2) Adjust autoscaling group or add GPU nodes with appropriate labels (nodeSelector: redwood/gpu=true).
  3) Drain and cordon old nodes if performing node replacement: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data.
- Backup & restore (artifacts + metadata):
  - Artifacts (models): snapshot object store to durable archive (S3 replication or on-prem tape as required).
  - Metadata (control plane DB): nightly logical backups and continuous WAL shipping. Restore procedure documented in Appendix C.

SLO monitoring and alerting (recommended):
- Uptime: control-plane API 99.95% monthly.
- Serving latency: p50 < 50ms (in-region, cached), p95 < 350ms (depends on model).
- Error budget: 0.05% allowed for control-plane API; alert at 10% burn in 24h window.

5) Upgrade and rollback procedures

Policy: upgrades are classified as patch (hotfix), minor (feature), and major (breaking). Customers should follow the recommended cadence: patch weekly, minor quarterly, major per contractual agreement. Always run staging or canary before fleet upgrades.

Pre-upgrade checklist:
- Run smoke tests against staging.
- Ensure backups of control-plane DB and object-store snapshots are available and verified.
- Verify no critical alerts and that error budget is within thresholds.
- Communicate maintenance window to stakeholders and register change in change-management system.

Upgrade steps (Helm example - minor release):
1. Create a canary namespace or tag: values.canary=true.
2. helm upgrade --install redwood-controlplane redwood/controlplane -n redwood -f values-canary.yaml --wait --timeout 15m
3. Run e2e smoke tests against canary (automated test suite) and monitor metrics for 30-60 minutes.
4. If OK, proceed with rolling upgrade: helm upgrade --install redwood-controlplane redwood/controlplane -n redwood -f values.yaml --wait --timeout 30m
5. Post-upgrade: run quick reconciliation and runbook validation (health checks).

Rollback (fast-path):
- If canary fails: rollback the canary release: helm rollback redwood-controlplane <prev-revision> -n redwood and investigate.
- If rolling upgrade fails and service degradation > defined threshold: initiate emergency rollback to prior Helm revision and restore DB snapshot if metadata is corrupted.

Rollforward vs rollback decision matrix (high-level):
- If data schema changed and incompatible => prefer rollback and restore from snapshot.
- If CPU/GPU scheduling regressions observed but no data corruption => consider rollforward with temporary capacity increase.

6) Customer requirements library (preflight questionnaire)

This section is a checklist to be completed with the customer during scoping. Items marked REQUIRED must be satisfied before scheduling a deployment.

Required items:
- Expected peak RPS / tokens-per-second and typical sequence length distribution.
- Desired latency SLOs (p50, p95) and availability SLA.
- Expected models (size, framework, quantized vs fp16) and artifact size footprint.
- Network topology: VPN/Direct Connect details, CIDR blocks, DNS control, and outbound egress constraints.
- Compliance requirements: data residency, retention, audit log retention period, and attestations required.
- KMS/HSM provider details and key rotation policy.
- Contact roster: technical contact, security contact, escalation contact with paging details.

Optional/Recommended items:
- Observability retention windows (metrics/logs/traces) and storage class preferences.
- Disaster recovery RTO/RPO targets and preferred DR test cadence.

7) Ownership and escalation

- Primary operator: customer SRE (day-to-day). Redwood is responsible for: installation QA, major-version upgrade guidance, and emergency support according to contract terms.
- On-call matrix: include Redwood on-call rotation for P1/P0 incidents during the first 90 days post-deployment (default onboarding window).
- Escalation path:
  1) Customer SRE -> Redwood Solutions Engineering (SE) -> Redwood Platform SRE -> Redwood Engineering (runtime team) -> Exec escalation.
  2) Use the dedicated incident channel and include runbooks and screenshots/timestamps.

8) Appendices

Appendix A: Example values.yaml (Helm) snippet:

nodeSelector:
  redwood/gpu: "true"
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: "4"
    memory: "16Gi"
  limits:
    cpu: "16"
    memory: "64Gi"
artifacts:
  s3_endpoint:
    url: "https://s3.example.corp"
    bucket: "redwood-models"
kms:
  provider: "aws-kms"
  key_id: "arn:aws:kms:us-west-2:111122223333:key/abcd-efgh"

Appendix B: Example IAM policy (cloud) - short form:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject"], "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::redwood-models/*"] }
  ]
}

Appendix C: Restore checklist (control plane DB)
1. Quiesce writes to control plane (scale replicas to 0 where applicable).
2. Restore DB from verified backup to staging cluster and run integrity checks.
3. Apply any migration scripts in dry-run mode and validate.
4. Promote restored DB to primary only after verification.

Common troubleshooting commands:
- kubectl -n redwood get pods -o wide
- kubectl logs <pod> -n redwood --tail=200
- nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,memory.total,utilization.gpu --format=csv
- aws s3 ls s3://redwood-models/ --endpoint-url=https://s3.example.corp

Document maintenance and feedback:
- Owner: eng-private-deployments team; update cadence: quarterly or on every major release.
- To propose changes, open a PR against the confluence source repository and add reviewers from the list in this doc.
